doc.title: Shelly Berg interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000

title: Breaking into Hollywood writing through relationships
summary: Film and rock work came through relationships; the Chicago big band album came via trombonist Jim Pankow, a Watrous fan.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: You mentioned writing for Hollywood and the studios. How did that come about? Do you need to meet people? Is there a way like —

My standard line is it’s a business of relationships, and all it takes is one. That’s another interesting thing is when you read interviews of film composers, well I was playing in some rock band and so-and-so became a fan and I did their student film and then they made it, and I mean it’s never I graduated from film scoring school and made phone calls and I got hired. Or they came and recruited me like lawyers. It’s totally relationships. Every cool job I’ve ever gotten has been from some convoluted path. And what I encourage my students to do, and people I talk to, is just be out there, be a musician, be playing, be where you can meet people. Because you never know what’s going to lead to what. I orchestrated an album for the pop band Chicago because the co-leader, Jim Panko, the trombone player is a big Bill Watrous fan and always came out to hear the band, and heard the orchestrations I did with Bill and said we’re going to do an album with a big band and I want you to write all the charts. And I’m going sure, like this will really happen. And it did. So it’s definitely a business of relationships. Some of the movie things I’ve done have come from rock things I’ve done, and the same rock producers have gotten involved in the movie industry and I’ve gotten in kind of that way. So that’s how it goes. There’s no path.
